# Book I, Proposition 4

*Two sides and the contained angle make the base equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><em>If two triangles have two sides (red and blue) and the angle they contain (yellow) equal, all the rest is equal too: the base (black), the other two angles (blue and red), and the triangles themselves.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/04.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.4, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.

I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,

and if the point A be placed on the point D

and the straight line AB on DE,

then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.

Again, AB coinciding with DE,

the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF;

hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.

But B also coincided with E;

hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.

[For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.

Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]

Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,

and will be equal to it.

And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to them,

the angle ABC to the angle DEF,

and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

Therefore etc.

(Being) what it was required to prove.

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop04.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop04.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where the statement already gives a step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Already given.** "For if, when B coincides with E and C with F…" Heiberg brackets this as an early scholium. A finite straight line enters our Lean only through its two ends, so once B is on E and C on F the base is EF, with no second one for the scholium to rule out.

```lean
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles
contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the
triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining
angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. -/
theorem Prop4 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hA : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F) :
    ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ ∧ △ A B C = △ D E F ∧ ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F ∧ ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE and AC to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF.
  have hBA : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hCA : C ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₃.symm
  have hCB : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hDEF.ne₁₂
  have hFE : F ≠ E := hDEF.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that the base BC is also equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC will be equal to the
  -- triangle DEF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively,
  -- namely those which the equal sides subtend, that is, the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and
  -- the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF,
  /- Euclid lays the triangle along the straight line DE, on the side where F
     is. Our superposition rule takes that line by name, and F off it. -/
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hF_DE : ¬ OnLine F DE := fun hF => hDEF ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hF⟩
  -- and if the point A be placed on the point D
  -- and the straight line AB on DE,
  /- This is superposition, the one rule that moves a figure (System E §3.7, in
     LeanEuclid's form). The triangle ABC, laid down with A on D, becomes the
     triangle DB'C': B' is on the ray from D through E, C' is on the same side
     of DE as F, and every side and angle is kept. -/
  obtain ⟨B', C', hB'_DE, hB'_ray, hC'_side, hDB', hB'C', hC'D, hB'DC', hDC'B', hC'B'D⟩ :=
    superposition hABC hD_DE hE_DE hDE hF_DE
  have hB'D : B' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq ((len_symm B' D).trans hDB') hBA.symm
  have hC'D' : C' ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hC'D hCA
  have hB'C'' : B' ≠ C' := ne_of_len_eq hB'C' hCB.symm
  -- then the point B will also coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE.
  /- The converse of C.N. 4 that Heath points out: on the ray from D through E,
     the one point as far from D as E is, is E itself. This is Savile's argument,
     `OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero. -/
  have hDB'_DE : ‖D B'‖ = ‖D E‖ := hDB'.trans hAB
  have hB'E : B' = E :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hDE, hB'D, ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE, hB'_DE⟩, hB'_ray⟩ hDB'_DE
  -- Again, AB coinciding with DE,
  have hEDC' : ∠ E D C' = ∠ B' D C' := CommonNotion4.angle hB'E.symm rfl rfl
  -- the straight line AC will also coincide with DF, because the angle BAC is equal to the
  -- angle EDF;
  have hEDC'_EDF : ∠ E D C' = ∠ E D F := hEDC'.trans (hB'DC'.trans hA)
  /- On F's side of DE only one ray from D makes this angle with DE
     (`onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero), so C' lies on the ray from D through F. -/
  have hC'_ray : OnRay C' D F :=
    onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hDE hD_DE hE_DE hC'_side) hEDC'_EDF
  -- hence the point C will also coincide with the point F, because AC is again equal to DF.
  have hDC'_DF : ‖D C'‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    (len_symm D C').trans (hC'D.trans ((len_symm C A).trans hAC))
  have hC'F : C' = F := OnRay.eq_of_len_eq hC'_ray hDC'_DF
  -- But B also coincided with E;
  -- hence the base BC will coincide with the base EF.
  -- [For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base
  -- EF, two straight lines will enclose a space: which is impossible.
  -- Therefore the base BC will coincide with EF] and will be equal to it. [C.N. 4]
  /- Heiberg brackets the words from "For if" to "EF" as an early scholium. A
     finite straight line enters our Lean only through its two ends, so once B'
     is E and C' is F the base B'C' is EF, and there is no second one on those
     ends for the scholium to rule out. C.N. 4 takes the ends alone; and B'C'
     has BC's length, since the moving keeps every side. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ := hB'C'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4 hB'E hC'F)
  -- Thus the whole triangle ABC will coincide with the whole triangle DEF,
  have hcoincide : △ D B' C' = △ D E F := CommonNotion4.triangle rfl hB'E hC'F
  -- and will be equal to it.
  /- Being moved does not change the triangle: DB'C' has the same sides and
     angles as ABC, so the same area (System E, Metric 9). -/
  have hmoved : △ A B C = △ D B' C' :=
    area_congruent hDB'.symm hB'C'.symm hC'D.symm
      ((angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans (hC'B'D.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'C''.symm hB'D.symm)))
      ((angle_symm hCB.symm hCA.symm).trans (hDC'B'.symm.trans (angle_symm hC'D'.symm hB'C'')))
      ((angle_symm hCA hBA).trans (hB'DC'.symm.trans (angle_symm hB'D hC'D')))
  have harea : △ A B C = △ D E F := hmoved.trans hcoincide
  -- And the remaining angles will also coincide with the remaining angles and will be equal to
  -- them,
  -- the angle ABC to the angle DEF,
  have hB : ∠ A B C = ∠ D E F :=
    (angle_symm hBA.symm hCB).trans
      (hC'B'D.symm.trans ((CommonNotion4.angle hC'F hB'E rfl).trans (angle_symm hFE hDE)))
  -- and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.
  have hC : ∠ A C B = ∠ D F E := hDC'B'.symm.trans (CommonNotion4.angle rfl hC'F hB'E)
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, harea, hB, hC⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to prove.
```

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

Euclid proves side–angle–side by picking up the triangle ABC and laying it down on DEF, and Heath thinks he did it unwillingly: "Euclid obviously used the method of superposition with reluctance" (vol. 1, p. 249). Jacques Peletier saw the danger in 1557. If superposition were allowed as a proof, Heath reports, it "could equally well have been used in I. 2, 3 (thus in I. 2 we could simply have supposed the line taken up and *placed* at the point)" (vol. 1, p. 249). So we let it in as one named rule, [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean), in LeanEuclid's form of System E §3.7, and Peletier's danger is real for it. A proof may build on the corners it places, so as a construction principle it is stronger than System E's rule, and only our policy keeps it to I.4 and I.8.

**Why must B land on E?** Heath points to something "most editors seem to have failed to observe": Euclid assumes that "if A be placed on D, and AB on DE, the point B will coincide with E, because AB is equal to DE. That is, the *converse* of *Common Notion* 4 is assumed for straight lines" (vol. 1, p. 250). Henry Savile closed the gap: "let B fall somewhere short of E or beyond E; and in either case it will follow that the less is equal to the greater, which is impossible" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 250). [Book Zero](../../Elements/Figure) has his argument, step for step, as `OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`.

AC falls along DF "because the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF", which assumes that on one side of DE only one ray from D makes that angle; Book Zero proves it as `onRay_of_angle_eq`, since otherwise one of two equal angles would be part of the other. The moving keeps every side and angle but says nothing of area, so that the triangle laid down is equal to ABC takes a rule of its own, [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean) (System E, Metric 9). The bases need no rule: Euclid's text says that otherwise "two straight lines will enclose a space", but J. L. Heiberg brackets the passage, since an-Nairīzī gives it after the Q. E. D., so it is "a *scholium* only" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 249). Once B lands on E and C on F, our base is EF.

**The modern way.** Superposition is a rigid motion: in the complex plane, $z \mapsto az + b$ or $z \mapsto a\bar{z} + b$ with $|a| = 1$, carrying A to D, B to E and C to F. What it carries is fixed by the two sides and the angle: the law of cosines, $\mathrm{BC}^2 = \mathrm{AB}^2 + \mathrm{AC}^2 - 2 \thinspace \mathrm{AB} \thinspace \mathrm{AC} \cos \mathrm{A}$, gives the base, and $\frac{1}{2} \thinspace \mathrm{AB} \thinspace \mathrm{AC} \sin \mathrm{A}$ the area.

## Further reading

- George E. Martin's [*Transformation Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-5680-9) (1982), a clear, step-by-step book, builds congruence itself out of reflections, and its ch. 5, "Congruence", shows superposition as a rigid motion.
- Where did the sine and cosine of the modern way come from? Eli Maor's [*Trigonometric Delights*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691202198/trigonometric-delights) (1998) tells it as a warm, story-filled history, from Egyptian pyramid slopes and Greek tables built from straight lines joining points on a circle to imaginary angles.
